article_title: Design and Implementation of the ESSA Resource Allocation Review: Lessons Learned in Utah
citation: Taylor, T., & Bowman, A. (2024). Design and Implementation of the ESSA Resource Allocation Review: Lessons Learned in Utah. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://web.stanford.edu/~mshanks/MichaelShanks/files/509554.pdf
title: Utah USBE resource allocation review process for schools eligible for comprehensive improvement support
description: The Utah State Board of Education, with WestEd's Region 15 Comprehensive Center, designed an RAR process beginning in March 2020 to help schools eligible for comprehensive improvement support. By "leveraging existing LEA and school-level data as well as required planning and reporting processes," USBE sought to support leaders in identifying and implementing strategies for equitable resource allocation, communicate scalable promising practices, align existing planning and reporting requirements, and build state capacity to connect identified needs, evidence-based strategies, and equitable resource allocation methods. The process was guided by principles of being comprehensive, collaborative, and systemic; minimizing burden on local agencies; and communicating the why for equity.
requirements: The process leverages existing LEA and school-level data and required planning and reporting processes rather than creating new ones.
constraints: The process was designed for schools eligible for comprehensive improvement support under ESSA, though the report recommends designing it so all LEAs and schools can participate regardless of improvement status.
target_learners: LEA and school leaders in Utah
target_learning_goals: identifying and addressing resource inequities to support school improvement
examples: USBE piloted and tested the process with LEAs and schools in spring 2023, and R15CC created an infographic describing an effective resource allocation review process.
key_sources: Taylor, T., & Bowman, A. (2024). Design and Implementation of the ESSA Resource Allocation Review: Lessons Learned in Utah. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://web.stanford.edu/~mshanks/MichaelShanks/files/509554.pdf

article_title: Refining Statewide School Accountability Systems: Lessons from Innovative State Approaches under ESSA
citation: Mitch Herz, Mel Wylen. (2025). Refining Statewide School Accountability Systems: Lessons From Innovative State Approaches Under ESSA. White paper.
title: Utah's Lowest Quartile (LQ) Growth Indicator
description: Utah's accountability model includes a growth indicator focused on the lowest performing 25 percent of students in each school, developed under the Next Generation School Accountability initiative and required by state statute (Utah Code 53E-5-205) as a measure of equitable educational opportunity. The paper explains, "Using student growth percentiles (SGPs), the LQ metric captures the share of students in a school's lowest quartile who achieved typical or better growth from one year to the next." This normative approach lets schools be recognized for helping all students progress, not just those near proficiency thresholds.
requirements: Technical metrics like SGPs must be paired with strong communication with interest holders
Multiyear processes of advisory input, technical refinement, and educator engagement
constraints: Reliance on SGPs created interpretation challenges, especially in schools where year-over-year group sizes vary; some parents and educators viewed the term lowest 25 percent as stigmatizing; the indicator is underutilized by community interest holders
target_learning_goals: academic growth of the lowest quartile of students and equitable educational opportunity
examples: The indicator was piloted and refined through Utah's Next Generation School Accountability vision with input from the Assessment and Accountability Policy Advisory Committee
key_sources: Mitch Herz, Mel Wylen. (2025). Refining Statewide School Accountability Systems: Lessons From Innovative State Approaches Under ESSA. White paper. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677595

article_title: Who Is Solving the Challenge? The Use of ChatGPT in Mathematics and Biology Courses Using Challenge-Based Learning
citation: Elizondo-García ME, Hernández-De la Cerda H, Benavides-García IG, Caratozzolo P and Membrillo-Hernández J (2025) Who is solving the challenge? The use of ChatGPT in mathematics and biology courses using challenge-based learning. Front. Educ. 10:1417642. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2025.1417642
title: UTAUT2-inspired 15-item survey instrument for assessing student perceptions of ChatGPT-assisted activities
description: A concluding survey administered after ChatGPT-assisted activities in both courses, comprising fifteen items: thirteen Likert-scale items (1–10) and two open questions. The Likert items were "inspired by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2) model" and aligned with critical thinking, instructional design, technology acceptance, and usage, grouped into three dimensions: Acceptance of the AI Tool (Q1–Q5), Instructional Design of the Learning Activity (Q6–Q7), and Critical Thinking (Q8–Q13). Items were filtered and consulted with experts in Psychology and Pedagogical Architects, who recommended them as sequential in analyzing students' perceptions when using ChatGPT.
requirements: Administered upon completion of the ChatGPT-assisted activity in the course
constraints: Items may seem repetitive; the article reports experts recommended them as sequential in analyzing perceptions
target_learners: higher education students in digital general-education STEM courses
target_learning_goals: student perceptions of AI-tool acceptance, instructional design quality, and critical thinking about AI outputs
examples: Used in the February–June 2023 pilot in Fundamentals of Biological Systems and Mathematics and Data Science for Decision Making
key_sources: Elizondo-García ME, Hernández-De la Cerda H, Benavides-García IG, Caratozzolo P and Membrillo-Hernández J (2025) Who is solving the challenge? The use of ChatGPT in mathematics and biology courses using challenge-based learning. Front. Educ. 10:1417642. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2025.1417642

article_title: Perceptions and Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence in Science Education Programmes: Voices of Pre-Service Science Teachers
citation: Amponsah, K. D., Adu-Boahen, J., Commey-Mintah, P., Kumassah, E. K., Ayittey, R. F., Nketsiah, J. (2026). Perceptions And Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence in Science Education Programmes: Voices of Pre-Service Science Teachers. Education Quarterly Reviews, 9(3), 51-65. https://doi.org/10.31014/aior.1993.09.03.724
title: Integrative UTAUT-TPB framework for AI adoption in science education
description: The study adapts the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (Venkatesh et al., 2003) and the Theory of Planned Behaviour (Ajzen, 1991) into an integrative framework in which "the influences of attitudes, norms, perceived behavioural control, and the performance and effort expected are channelled primarily through behavioural intention". UTAUT supplies performance expectancy and effort expectancy; TPB supplies attitude and perceived behavioural control; behavioural intention sits closest to behaviour. The authors argue UTAUT alone is "good at predicting a person's intention but weak at explaining the behaviour", motivating the integration.
requirements: Measurement of performance expectancy, effort expectancy, attitude, perceived behavioural control, behavioural intention, and actual use as distinct constructs
constraints: The article notes UTAUT alone is weak at explaining behaviour once intention is formed, motivating the TPB integration
target_learning_goals: technology acceptance and integration of AI in science teaching
examples: The study measured the six constructs with a structured questionnaire whose reliability and validity were confirmed (Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability above 0.70, AVE above 0.50 for all constructs).
key_sources: Amponsah, K. D., Adu-Boahen, J., Commey-Mintah, P., Kumassah, E. K., Ayittey, R. F., Nketsiah, J. (2026). Perceptions And Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence in Science Education Programmes: Voices of Pre-Service Science Teachers. Education Quarterly Reviews, 9(3), 51-65. https://doi.org/10.31014/aior.1993.09.03.724

article_title: AI Adoption Among Teachers: Insights on Concerns, Support, Confidence, and Attitudes
citation: Vanessa Baltazar Sibug, Maria Anna David Cruz, Vicky Pineda Vital, Juvy Cruz Grume, Almer Balingit Gamboa, Emerson Quiambao Fernando, Lloyd David Feliciano, Jordan Lansang Salenga, and John Paul Palo Miranda. 2025. AI Adoption Among Teachers: Insights on Concerns, Support, Confidence, and Attitudes. In 2025 the 9th International Conference on Education and Multimedia Technology (ICEMT) (ICEMT 2025), July 29–August 01, 2025, Osaka, Japan. ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://doi.org/10.1145/3761843.3761881
title: UTAUT-based framing of AI adoption: institutional support as facilitating condition, confidence as self-efficacy, concerns as inhibitors, attitudes as behavioral intention
description: The study grounds its analysis in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), mapping its four measured constructs onto UTAUT constructs. As the article states, it "defines institutional support as a facilitating condition, confidence as self-efficacy, concerns as inhibitors, and attitudes as behavioral intention." The analysis extends UTAUT by exploring how institutional and psychological factors jointly shape AI adoption in teaching, using moderated regression and mediation to test the mapped relationships.
requirements: The framework requires measuring the four constructs (institutional support, confidence, concerns, attitudes) with validated multi-item scales, here a 35-item five-point Likert instrument checked by two educational technology experts
constraints: The article applies the framework to teachers in Pampanga, Philippines, sampled purposively across educational levels
target_learning_goals: teacher readiness for AI integration and technology adoption
examples: The study operationalized the four UTAUT-mapped constructs in a 35-item Likert survey and tested them with moderated multiple regression and mediation analysis

article_title: Decoding symmetric and asymmetric pathways in generative AI learning adoption: a multi-method study
citation: Xin Tian, Musa Adekunle Ayanwale, Rethabile Rosemary Molefi, Preeti Manchanda, Nurgün Gençel and Barakat Olabisi Ogunjoun. (2026). Decoding symmetric and asymmetric pathways in generative AI learning adoption: a multi-method study. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00613-w
title: Integrated UTAUT3–ARCS hybrid-logic framework of Gen-AI adoption
description: The article integrates the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT3) with Keller's ARCS Motivation Model into a dual-layer account of Gen-AI adoption. UTAUT3 answers "Can I use this technology effectively?", whereas ARCS answers "Will I continue to engage with it for learning?". The framework posits a hybrid logic in which cognitive beliefs enable acceptance, motivational experiences sustain engagement, and habitual interaction normalizes use; ARCS is positioned as a motivational layer that reinforces or undermines cognitive evaluations and the pathway from intention to use.
requirements: Measurement of both acceptance beliefs (PE, EE, SI, FC, HM, HB, PI) and the four ARCS dimensions as distinct constructs, with satisfaction treated as an outcome-based evaluation distinct from hedonic motivation and habit
constraints: Tested in a low-resource higher education context (Lesotho) with cross-sectional data, so structural paths are interpreted as theory-consistent associations rather than definitive causal effects
target_learners: Higher education students in resource-constrained settings who have prior experience using ChatGPT or similar Gen-AI tools for academic work
target_learning_goals: Sustained adoption and use of generative AI tools for academic learning tasks
examples: The study operationalized the framework with ten constructs on a six-point Likert scale, validated via expert review (S-CVI/Ave = 0.94) and MGRM-IRT, and tested it with PLS-SEM, NCA, fsQCA, and machine learning on data from 842 Lesotho students
key_sources: Xin Tian, Musa Adekunle Ayanwale, Rethabile Rosemary Molefi, Preeti Manchanda, Nurgün Gençel and Barakat Olabisi Ogunjoun. (2026). Decoding symmetric and asymmetric pathways in generative AI learning adoption: a multi-method study. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00613-w

title: Consolidating AI risk management frameworks with utilitarian ethics for responsible generative AI use
description: This account proposes that organisations manage generative AI risks by combining the NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework with utilitarian ethical reasoning. The NIST framework "can guide the organisations developing, adopting, and implementing AI solutions to systematically assess, understand, and manage risks", with risks mapped to the context of use. Utilitarianism then supplies "a flexible result-oriented lens for formulating and testing policies at each stage of the risk management cycle", prioritising impacts on each stakeholder. The article argues the two should be consolidated so decisions about ChatGPT design, adoption and evolution provide the most good or least harm for society.
requirements: Ethical reviews and bias screening complementing periodic risk assessments because the algorithm is evolutionary in nature
Responsible AI toolkits and frameworks embedding ethical perspectives
constraints: Risks related to ChatGPT adoption should be mapped to its specific context of use and application
Risk stems from the quality, authenticity and reliability of training data and human rectification
target_learners: Organisations, AI developers and policy makers adopting generative AI
target_learning_goals: Ethical decision-making and responsible use of generative AI tools
examples: The article suggests assessing ChatGPT adoption risks with the RMF while prioritising stakeholder impacts using the utilitarian perspective, weighing whether adoption promotes welfare compared to alternatives

article_title: Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources
citation: Kyong Mi Choi, Jin Mun, Brian Hand. (2026). Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10115-2
title: Utilization of resources: reasoning as selectively activated intellectual resource rather than transferred skill
description: This framework reconceptualizes cross-domain reasoning not as direct transfer of skills but as utilization—the active deployment of intellectual resources across contextual boundaries. Drawing on diSessa's knowledge in pieces, Hammer et al.'s resources framework, Bailin's reasoning-as-practice, and situated learning theory, the article treats procedural knowledge in the applying domain as an assemblage of cognitive resources that learners "strategically mobilized and adapted" for reasoning tasks. It guides the study's hypothesis that applying components are foundational resources selectively activated during reasoning.
requirements: Reasoning is treated as domain-embedded practice coordinated with background knowledge, standards of inquiry, heuristic strategies, and habits of mind rather than isolated technical competencies
constraints: The article distinguishes this lens from transfer frameworks, noting transfer attempts predicated on superficial similarity can precipitate negative transfer
target_learners: K-12 mathematics and science students assessed in TIMSS
target_learning_goals: Cross-domain reasoning in mathematics and science
examples: The study analyzes TIMSS applying and reasoning components as candidate intellectual resources supporting reasoning across mathematics and science
key_sources: Kyong Mi Choi, Jin Mun, Brian Hand. (2026). Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10115-2

article_title: Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention
citation: Carol Sansone, K. Ann Renninger, Judith M. Harackiewicz. (2026). Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10142-7
title: Framework: effects of generating utility value on motivation differ by phase of interest development depending on compatibility of useful and interesting content
description: The article's integrative framework hypothesizes that generating utility value affects motivation differently at earlier and later phases of interest. Figure 1 "displays the hypothesized effect of generating utility value for course content on students' motivation to engage with that content" and illustrates that "useful content may align with interest at earlier phases of interest but may diverge at later phases of interest." At earlier phases, perceived utility and interest can work in sync; at later phases, divergence between useful and interesting content can create conflict about where to invest effort, while compatibility is mutually reinforcing.
requirements: Understanding the effects requires considering the degree to which the learning content perceived as useful is compatible with the content that is the focus of developing interest
constraints: The framework is hypothesized; the article states exploration of these questions requires data capturing students' perceptions, feelings, and behaviors over time, and the nature of differences in how students with more developed interest regulate motivation are not yet known
target_learners: high school and college students in courses with required content
target_learning_goals: motivation to engage with course content and sustained engagement over time
examples: A student may generate utility for fungi as food or brewing beer without wanting to learn more, while the 'wood wide web' possibility triggers interest with little immediate practical use
key_sources: Carol Sansone, K. Ann Renninger, Judith M. Harackiewicz. (2026). Motivating Self-Regulation: Utility Value, Interest Development, and the Potential for Intervention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10142-7

article_title: Another 25 Years of AIED? Challenges and Opportunities for Intelligent Educational Technologies of the Future
citation: Niels Pinkwart. (2016). Another 25 Years of AIED? Challenges and Opportunities for Intelligent Educational Technologies of the Future. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:771–783. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0099-7
title: Utopian and dystopian future scenarios as an analytic device for envisioning AIED's future
description: The paper constructs two contrasting narrative scenarios—students Ana and Ben in a utopian future and Dan and Eve in a dystopian one—as a deliberation device. The author states the scenarios, which are admittedly extreme, may "serve as a means for thinking about possible futures of AIED and about decisions that AIED researchers and developers might be faced with in the future." The device grounds the derivation of the seven challenges and frames them as risks and opportunities rather than predictions.
requirements: External trends in technology, education, and educational technology must first be listed as relatively stable states or development trends
constraints: The author notes there is no way any of these visions can be right or wrong in a scientific way, and no way to prove or falsify them now
target_learners: secondary school students nearing graduation as depicted in the scenarios
target_learning_goals: anticipating future directions of AIED research and deployment
examples: A dialogue-based utopia with privacy-respecting lifelong tutors and a dystopia with commercial data-selling tutors and teacher layoffs
key_sources: Niels Pinkwart. (2016). Another 25 Years of AIED? Challenges and Opportunities for Intelligent Educational Technologies of the Future. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:771–783. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0099-7

article_title: Exploring the Long-Term Effects of the Statewide Implementation of an Automated Writing Evaluation System on Students’ State Test ELA Performance
citation: Yue Huang, Joshua Wilson, & Henry May. (2024). Exploring the Long-Term Effects of the Statewide Implementation of an Automated Writing Evaluation System on Students' State Test ELA Performance. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00443-9
title: Utah Compose (UC), a statewide automated writing evaluation system with the PEG scoring engine and interpretable partially connected neural networks
description: Utah Compose is a web-based AWE system developed by Measurement Incorporated, implemented statewide in Utah from Fall 2014, providing "unlimited access to pre-designed prompts aligned with different grade levels and writing genres" plus automated scores and instant revision feedback. It uses the PEG scoring engine built on "800 + linguistic variables" and trains models for six writing traits across three genres and five grade bands, with human-machine agreement reported at a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.835 (SD = 0.026). For interpretability, UC "employs neural networks with selectively connected hidden nodes" matching pre-classified linguistic feature groups so revision improves scores, plus peer review, tutorials, and graphic organizers.
requirements: Trained on a diverse sample of essays scored by well-trained human raters, with generalization evaluated on a separate held-out test dataset
constraints: Implementation was naturalistic: no state-mandated usage and no uniform professional development for teachers
target_learning_goals: Writing proficiency and improvement through practice, immediate feedback, and guided instructional support
examples: State-contracted tool of the Utah State Board of Education starting Fall 2014; the Utah-branded equivalent of MI Write
key_sources: Yue Huang, Joshua Wilson, & Henry May. (2024). Exploring the Long-Term Effects of the Statewide Implementation of an Automated Writing Evaluation System on Students' State Test ELA Performance. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00443-9

article_title: Co-producing AIED Ethics Under Lockdown: an Empirical Study of Deliberative Democracy in Action
citation: Teresa Swist, Simon Buckingham Shum, Kalervo N. Gulson. (2024). Co-producing AIED Ethics Under Lockdown: an Empirical Study of Deliberative Democracy in Action. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 34:670–705. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00380-z
title: UTS EdTech Ethics Deliberative Democracy consultation
description: A university-wide DD consultation at the University of Technology Sydney, run under pandemic lockdown, co-producing ethical principles to govern Analytics/AI-enabled Educational Technology (AAI-EdTech). The brief asked: "What principles should govern UTS use of analytics and artificial intelligence to improve teaching and learning for all, while minimising the possibility of harmful outcomes?" A DMP of 20 was recruited from 131 applicants through stratified sampling and committed to a 5-part workshop series over seven weeks, using Zoom, Google Docs and Basecamp, with guest experts and iterative principle drafting.
requirements: A suitably open-ended but tractable brief with a clear deliverable
Participant commitment to the full workshop series
External DD facilitator working with an institutional planning team
constraints: Conducted entirely online under lockdown conditions
Recruitment mitigates but does not eliminate sampling bias, with an inherent response bias towards people willing to engage
target_learning_goals: co-producing ethical principles for AAI-EdTech
informed deliberation about values and expectations for educational data use
examples: Session 3 produced a work-in-progress draft sent to stakeholders and experts; in the closing workshop four DMP members elected by peers presented revised principles to three senior leaders
key_sources: Teresa Swist, Simon Buckingham Shum, Kalervo N. Gulson. (2024). Co-producing AIED Ethics Under Lockdown: an Empirical Study of Deliberative Democracy in Action. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 34:670–705. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00380-z

article_title: Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review.
citation: Esmaeel T, Elham T, Fereidooni Mahsa, Ayatollahi Haleh. (2024). Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review. Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-024-02723-w
title: UTAUT as an organizing framework for factors influencing acceptance and use of XR in surgical training
description: The article uses the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) as its guiding framework for synthesizing findings across 44 included reviews. It states that the model "has four domains including performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions which offer valuable insights into the drivers and barriers faced by users." The review coded findings from the included systematic reviews into these four domains using qualitative software.
requirements: Findings from included reviews must be codable into the four UTAUT domains of performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions
constraints: The review reports significant heterogeneity across included studies, which precluded quantitative meta-analysis and required a qualitative framework synthesis
target_learning_goals: surgical skill acquisition
technology adoption in surgical training
examples: Two authors independently coded findings from the 44 included reviews using MAXQDA, categorizing them under the four UTAUT domains.
key_sources: Esmaeel T, Elham T, Fereidooni Mahsa, Ayatollahi Haleh. (2024). Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review. Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-024-02723-w

article_title: Analysis of Tools Used in Assessing Technical Skills and Operative Competence in Trauma and Orthopaedic Surgical Training: A Systematic Review.
citation: James H.K., Chapman A.W., Pattison G.T.R., Fisher J.D., Griffin D.R. (2020). Analysis of Tools Used in Assessing Technical Skills and Operative Competence in Trauma and Orthopaedic Surgical Training: A Systematic Review. JBJS Reviews. https://doi.org/10.2106/JBJS.RVW.19.00167
title: Van Der Vleuten's utility index for evaluating assessment instruments
description: The utility index is a widely accepted framework, described by Van Der Vleuten, for appraising an evaluation instrument. The review uses it to appraise each technical skills-assessment tool, defining validity (with content, construct, and concurrent subtypes), reliability, feasibility/acceptability, educational impact, and cost-effectiveness. The authors state it is "a widely accepted framework for assessing an evaluation instrument" and summarize evidence for each tool against these criteria.
requirements: Assessment tools must be appraised across validity, reliability, feasibility/acceptability, and educational impact dimensions to establish utility evidence.
constraints: Cost-effectiveness was not evaluated in this review.
target_learners: postgraduate surgical residents in trauma and orthopaedics
target_learning_goals: technical surgical skill and operative competence assessment
examples: Each of the assessment tools in the review's Appendix Table 3 was appraised for utility against the index criteria in columns 5 to 11.
key_sources: James H.K., Chapman A.W., Pattison G.T.R., Fisher J.D., Griffin D.R. (2020). Analysis of Tools Used in Assessing Technical Skills and Operative Competence in Trauma and Orthopaedic Surgical Training: A Systematic Review. JBJS Reviews. https://doi.org/10.2106/JBJS.RVW.19.00167

article_title: When Assessment Theory Meets Generative AI: Reimagining SBA Design in Medical Education.
citation: Al-Shawee N, McElvaney G, Strawbridge J, Spooner M. (2026). When Assessment Theory Meets Generative AI: Reimagining SBA Design in Medical Education. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2033
title: Van der Vleuten's Utility Index applied to GenAI-assisted SBA item-writing: five multiplicatively interacting dimensions
description: The article applies Van der Vleuten's Utility Index — validity, reliability, educational impact, acceptability, and cost-efficiency — as the theoretical lens for evaluating GenAI integration into item-writing. The dimensions "interact multiplicatively, meaning that a weakness in any single domain can compromise the overall quality of assessment." Table 1 maps each dimension to potential challenges and benefits of GenAI co-created items, e.g. structured prompts ensuring curricular alignment for validity and chain-of-thought reasoning supporting educational impact.
requirements: Each dimension is essential to overall utility; balance must be maintained across all five
constraints: GenAI's speed and scalability could, if not managed carefully, inadvertently weaken other domains
target_learning_goals: Evaluating assessment quality of AI-assisted item development
examples: Table 1 notes GenAI's capacity to generate large numbers of items quickly can increase cost-efficiency and consistency (reliability), while curriculum-agnostic generation risks misalignment

article_title: The impact of DeepSeek's perceived interactivity on medical students' self-directed learning ability.
citation: Ju Yubin, Li Jingwei, Zhang Xiaopeng, Wu Meijie, Pang Xinyu, Li Zhengyu, Wang Junyang, Li Jiaxin, Zhang Yuanyuan, Dai Xin. (2026). The impact of DeepSeek's perceived interactivity on medical students' self-directed learning ability. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-33780-3
title: Extended UTAUT-SCT-TTF integrated model of generative AI adoption and self-directed learning
description: The article constructs a multilevel research framework integrating three theoretical models — UTAUT (performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence), Task-Technology Fit (task and technology characteristics), and Social Cognitive Theory (self-efficacy) — with trust added as a moderator and self-efficacy as a mediator. It states: "This study integrates the UTAUT, SCT, and TTF frameworks to construct a multidimensional theoretical model that systematically reveals the mechanism through which the perceived interactivity of generative AI (DeepSeek) influences medical students'autonomous learning abilities." The rationale is that UTAUT alone has limited explanatory power for professional context and learning outcomes, TTF addresses task-technology fit, and SCT supplies the psychological mechanism linking use to skill enhancement.
requirements: Measured constructs for perceived interactivity, expectancies, social influence, task-technology fit, trust, self-efficacy, behavioral intention, and self-directed learning ability, each with at least three measurement items
constraints: The article notes UTAUT has limited explanatory power regarding professional context adaptability and learning outcomes, motivating the integration
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning ability
technology acceptance of generative AI tools

article_title: Exploring the Role of Immersive Virtual Reality Simulation in Health Professions Education: Thematic Analysis.
citation: Jordan Talan, MHPE, MD; Forster Molly, MD; Joseph Leian, MD; Pradhan Deepak, MHPE, MD. (2025). Exploring the Role of Immersive Virtual Reality Simulation in Health Professions Education: Thematic Analysis. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/62803
title: Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) as a framework for studying VR simulation adoption
description: UTAUT2 explains factors affecting adoption of new technologies and predicts future technology use. The original theory described 4 constructs as direct determinants of technology usage behavior: performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions, modified by gender, age, or experience; UTAUT2 added hedonic motivation, price value, and habit. The authors used UTAUT2 as the a priori coding lens for directed content analysis of early-adopter interviews, finding it distinguishes features of VR technology from other modes of simulation and supports predicting future use.
requirements: A priori codes defined through the lens of the UTAUT2 theoretical framework, followed by an exploratory coding phase
constraints: The UTAUT was initially described in the individual consumer marketplace, which the authors suggest may limit fit for educational technology contexts
target_learners: health professions educators and early adopters of VR simulation
target_learning_goals: understanding and predicting adoption of immersive VR simulation technology in educational practice
examples: The study applied UTAUT2 in a directed content analysis of 16 semistructured interviews, generating 38 unique codes and four themes mapped onto the framework
